Let the polygon have \(m=2n+1\) vertices, labeled clockwise.

For any three chosen vertices, look at the three clockwise arcs between consecutive chosen vertices. If their lengths in number of sides are \(a,b,c\), then

\[
a+b+c=2n+1,
\]

with \(a,b,c\ge 1\).

The center of the polygon is the circumcenter of the triangle. The center lies inside the triangle exactly when the triangle is acute. An interior angle subtends the opposite arc, so the angles are

\[
\frac{\pi a}{2n+1},\quad \frac{\pi b}{2n+1},\quad \frac{\pi c}{2n+1}.
\]

Since \(2n+1\) is odd, no arc can be exactly half the circle. Thus the triangle is acute exactly when

\[
a,b,c\le n.
\]

So the center is outside exactly when one of \(a,b,c\) is at least \(n+1\). Such a gap is unique, since two gaps of size at least \(n+1\) would sum to more than \(2n+1\).

Now count the bad choices. Suppose the unique large gap ends at vertex \(V\). Then the other two chosen vertices must lie among the next \(n\) vertices clockwise from \(V\). Conversely, choosing any two of those \(n\) vertices gives a unique large gap back to \(V\).

Thus the number of bad triples is

\[
(2n+1)\binom{n}{2}.
\]

The total number of triples is

\[
\binom{2n+1}{3}.
\]

Therefore the desired probability is

\[
1-\frac{(2n+1)\binom{n}{2}}{\binom{2n+1}{3}}.
\]

Compute:

\[
\binom{2n+1}{3}=\frac{(2n+1)(2n)(2n-1)}{6},
\]

\[
(2n+1)\binom{n}{2}=(2n+1)\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.
\]

So

\[
P
=
1-\frac{(2n+1)\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}
{\frac{(2n+1)(2n)(2n-1)}{6}}
\]

\[
=
1-\frac{3n(n-1)}{2n(2n-1)}
\]

\[
=
\frac{2n(2n-1)-3n(n-1)}{2n(2n-1)}
\]

\[
=
\frac{n^2+n}{2n(2n-1)}
=
\frac{n+1}{2(2n-1)}.
\]

Thus the probability is

\[
\boxed{\frac{n+1}{2(2n-1)}}.
\]
